name: Bloom Energy
constraint_controlled: Bloom manufactures and deploys solid oxide fuel cell systems that deliver on-site power to data centers in 12-18 months, bypassing the 5-7 year grid interconnection queue.
physics_thesis: Bloom is one of the few commercially-scaled solutions that lets hyperscalers bring AI training capacity online without waiting for utility grid connections, which are now the binding constraint on AI buildout. Their SOFC technology is differentiated, vertically manufactured, and already contracted with AEP, Equinix, and Oracle. The physics arbitrage is real: they bypass the grid queue with a manufacturable product competitors cannot replicate quickly.
key_metrics: MW of data center backlog/bookings; product gross margin; deployment lead time vs grid queue
reasoning: Bloom directly manufactures and owns the IP/factory for SOFC stacks — a genuine physical product addressing the grid bottleneck — earning a high ownership score, though it's an equipment OEM rather than an irreplaceable resource holder. Supply response is moderate-to-slow because SOFC manufacturing capacity, ceramic stack production, and permitting take 2-5 years to scale, but unlike uranium or copper it is ultimately a manufacturable good.

name: Vistra Energy
constraint_controlled: Vistra owns ~41 GW of dispatchable generation including 6.4 GW of nuclear capacity (Comanche Peak and the Energy Harbor fleet) plus large gas and coal fleets with existing grid interconnections.
physics_thesis: Vistra controls one of the largest fleets of already-interconnected, dispatchable baseload power in the US, including four nuclear reactors that are physically irreplaceable on any reasonable AI buildout timeline. Hyperscalers are signing behind-the-meter and PPA deals directly with nuclear operators (cf. Amazon-Talen, Microsoft-Constellation), and Vistra's nuclear plus ERCOT gas footprint makes it a prime counterparty. New nuclear takes 10+ years and new large gas plants face 5-7 year interconnection queues, so existing GW are the scarce asset.
key_metrics: Nuclear PPA announcements and pricing ($/MWh); ERCOT and PJM forward power curves; uncontracted nuclear/gas GW available for hyperscaler deals
reasoning: Ownership is 9 because Vistra physically owns and operates a large nuclear fleet plus interconnected gas capacity — direct control of the exact asset hyperscalers need, with only a handful of peers (Constellation, Talen, NextEra). Supply response is 9 because new nuclear is a 10+ year build and new large interconnected thermal capacity is 5-10 years even with unlimited capital, so the existing fleet cannot be meaningfully replicated near-term.

name: Constellation Energy
constraint_controlled: Largest US nuclear fleet (~22 GW) of operating, licensed, carbon-free baseload generation directly contractable by hyperscalers.
physics_thesis: Constellation owns the largest fleet of operating nuclear reactors in the US — irreplaceable 24/7 carbon-free baseload that AI hyperscalers are signing decade-plus PPAs for (e.g. Three Mile Island restart with Microsoft). New nuclear takes 10+ years and faces NRC licensing, fuel, and supply chain bottlenecks, so existing licensed gigawatts are effectively un-replicable on the AI buildout timeline. This is a textbook physics arbitrage: scarce, licensed, already-connected baseload power.
key_metrics: GW contracted to hyperscalers via PPAs; realized $/MWh on data center contracts; license extensions and uprate MW added
reasoning: Ownership is a 10 because CEG physically operates the largest licensed nuclear fleet in the US — geologically/regulatorily irreplaceable assets with no substitute for 24/7 clean baseload. Supply response is a 10 because new nuclear capacity requires 10+ years for licensing and construction even with unlimited capital, and SMRs are not yet commercially deployed at scale.

name: NRG Energy
constraint_controlled: NRG owns and operates ~13 GW of dispatchable generation capacity (gas, coal) primarily in ERCOT/Texas, plus a large retail electricity customer book.
physics_thesis: NRG controls existing, interconnected generation capacity in Texas — the most AI-data-center-hungry grid in the US — at a moment when new generation queues are 5+ years long. Its retail platform also positions it to sign long-term PPAs with hyperscalers seeking firm power. However, its fleet is largely gas/coal with retail services (Vivint) diluting the pure-play physics angle.
key_metrics: MW of dispatchable capacity in ERCOT; hyperscaler PPA announcements; ERCOT forward power prices
reasoning: Ownership score of 6 because NRG directly operates physical generation assets behind grid interconnects (a real bottleneck), but multiple IPP competitors exist (Vistra, Constellation, Talen) and a meaningful chunk of revenue is retail/smart home services rather than pure generation. Supply response of 7 reflects that new gas plants take 3-5 years and grid interconnection queues stretch 5-7 years, so existing capacity is genuinely scarce but not as irreplaceable as nuclear or uranium.

name: Core Scientific
constraint_controlled: Owns and operates ~1.2GW of energized, grid-connected data center power capacity across multiple US sites that can be converted from Bitcoin mining to AI/HPC hosting.
physics_thesis: Core Scientific controls something AI hyperscalers physically cannot get for 5-7 years: large-scale, already-energized grid interconnections. The CoreWeave 12-year, $10B+ contract validates that pre-connected power sites are the binding constraint for AI buildout. New interconnects of this scale face multi-year ISO queues regardless of capital deployed.
key_metrics: Contracted AI/HPC power capacity (MW); CoreWeave contract revenue realization; Incremental MW energized per quarter
reasoning: Core Scientific is the canonical example in this framework — it physically owns and operates the scarcest asset in the AI buildout: gigawatts of pre-existing grid interconnection. Ownership scores 9 (not 10) because a handful of other Bitcoin miners hold similar pre-connected sites. Supply response is 8 because replicating 1GW+ of new grid interconnect takes 5-7 years minimum even with unlimited capital, due to ISO queues and transmission constraints.

name: TeraWulf
constraint_controlled: TeraWulf owns and operates the Lake Mariner site in upstate New York with ~750 MW of grid-connected power (zero-carbon, nuclear/hydro-fed) being converted from bitcoin mining to AI/HPC hosting, with multi-hundred-MW leases signed to Core42/Fluidstack/Google.
physics_thesis: WULF directly controls a scarce physical asset that AI hyperscalers desperately need: pre-existing, energized grid interconnection at a single campus capable of scaling past 1 GW. Replicating this from scratch requires 5-7 years of utility queue time plus substation, transformer, and zoning work — capital cannot compress this. As a converter of crypto-era power into AI hosting, it sits in the same physics-arbitrage bucket as CORZ.
key_metrics: Contracted MW of HPC capacity (and lease economics $/kW); Lake Mariner energized capacity expansion schedule; counterparty quality and lease tenor of hyperscaler contracts
reasoning: Ownership 8 because WULF physically owns and operates the Lake Mariner site with energized, low-carbon interconnection — a genuinely scarce asset with limited replicability — though it is one of several pre-connected miners (CORZ, IREN, CIFR) competing for the same thesis, keeping it below 9-10. Supply response 8 because new comparable sites require 5-7+ years of grid queue, transformer procurement, and permitting — unlimited capital cannot meaningfully accelerate the ISO interconnection process.

name: Iris Energy
constraint_controlled: Owns and operates ~2.9 GW of secured grid-connected power capacity at data center sites in Texas and British Columbia, with operational substations and energized infrastructure.
physics_thesis: IREN controls pre-connected, energized power capacity — the single scarcest input for AI training, with grid interconnection queues now running 5-7 years in ERCOT and most North American utilities. The company is actively converting Bitcoin mining sites to AI/HPC hosting (Childress, Sweetwater) with liquid-cooled GPU deployments, leveraging existing substations and PPAs that cannot be replicated quickly. Like CORZ, the physics arbitrage is owning energized megawatts today rather than waiting for new interconnects.
key_metrics: Energized MW capacity and AI/HPC contracted MW; AI cloud + colocation revenue run-rate; GPU fleet size and utilization
reasoning: Ownership score 8 because IREN directly owns the land, substations, and grid interconnections — a genuinely scarce physical asset with 5-7 year replication time — though it competes with several other miner-to-AI converts (CORZ, CIFR, APLD, WULF). Supply response 8 because new grid-connected gigawatt-scale sites take 5-7+ years to permit, interconnect, and energize regardless of capital.

name: Applied Digital
constraint_controlled: Operates data center sites in North Dakota with secured power capacity (400MW+ at Ellendale) and grid interconnects for HPC/AI hosting.
physics_thesis: Applied Digital pivoted from crypto hosting to AI/HPC hosting, leveraging already-energized sites with power purchase agreements that bypass multi-year grid interconnection queues. Their Ellendale campus has signed a long-term lease with CoreWeave, validating the pre-connected power thesis. The bottleneck they control is energized, build-ready land — scarce in the current AI buildout.
key_metrics: Contracted MW capacity leased to hyperscalers; Ellendale campus build-out progress; lease revenue and tenant credit quality (CoreWeave)
reasoning: APLD directly operates physical data center infrastructure with pre-secured power, similar to CORZ — earning a 7 on ownership since they own/operate the asset but face competition from other repurposed crypto sites and hyperscaler-owned campuses. Supply response is 7 because new sites with comparable power take 2-5 years to interconnect, though APLD's specific edge is narrower than uranium or nuclear assets.

name: Riot Platforms
constraint_controlled: Riot operates large-scale, grid-connected power capacity at its Rockdale (Texas) and Corsicana facilities, totaling ~1+ GW of contracted/energized power that bypasses multi-year interconnection queues.
physics_thesis: Riot owns and operates Bitcoin mining sites with already-energized substations and ERCOT interconnects — exactly the scarce 'pre-connected power' that hyperscalers now need for AI training. Its Corsicana site (up to 1 GW) is one of the largest single-site power buildouts in North America and could be partially converted to HPC/AI hosting, similar to the CORZ playbook. The Engineering segment (E4A Solutions) also manufactures power distribution equipment, adding modest grid-infrastructure exposure.
key_metrics: Energized MW capacity and interconnection status at Corsicana; AI/HPC hosting contract announcements or co-location deals; power cost per kWh and PPA structure
reasoning: Ownership score 7 because Riot directly owns and operates physical, grid-connected power sites — a genuine bottleneck — but it has not yet converted to AI hosting and faces several peer miners (CORZ, IREN, CIFR, WULF) with similar pre-connected power; it is not the dominant operator. Supply response score 7 reflects that replicating a 1 GW ERCOT-interconnected site takes 4-7 years given transformer lead times and interconnection queues, though Texas is faster than most US grids.

name: Marathon Digital
constraint_controlled: Owns and operates large-scale energized data center sites with grid-connected power capacity (~1+ GW) currently used for Bitcoin mining, convertible to AI/HPC hosting.
physics_thesis: MARA directly owns and operates power-energized data center infrastructure that bypasses the 5-7 year grid interconnection queue strangling AI buildout. Like CORZ, its Bitcoin mining footprint represents pre-connected megawatts that can be repurposed for AI inference/training colocation. However, its sites are often less suited to high-density GPU compute than peers (older air-cooled designs, remote locations), and the AI pivot is earlier-stage than CORZ's CoreWeave deal.
key_metrics: Energized MW capacity owned vs hosted; AI/HPC revenue mix and contracted hyperscaler deals; PUE and liquid-cooling retrofit capex
reasoning: Ownership score of 7 reflects direct physical operation of grid-connected power sites — a real bottleneck asset — but tempered by competition from CORZ, IREN, CIFR, RIOT, WULF and questions about site suitability for dense AI workloads. Supply response of 6 reflects that new grid-connected gigawatt sites take 2-5 years to build and energize, though existing miners worldwide create some near-term substitutes for the pre-connected power thesis.

name: Eaton Corporation
constraint_controlled: Eaton manufactures medium- and low-voltage switchgear, transformers, busways, and power distribution units that data centers physically cannot operate without.
physics_thesis: AI data centers require massive electrical distribution infrastructure — switchgear, transformers, PDUs — and Eaton is one of a small handful of suppliers (with Schneider, ABB, Siemens) with the manufacturing capacity and certifications to deliver at hyperscale. Lead times for large switchgear have stretched to 50-80+ weeks, signaling real physical scarcity. However, Eaton manufactures equipment rather than owning a unique physical asset, and has multiple credible global competitors, capping the ownership score.
key_metrics: Electrical Americas backlog and book-to-bill; switchgear/transformer lead times; data center vertical revenue mix
reasoning: Ownership score 6: Eaton physically manufactures bottlenecked grid equipment but is one of 4-5 global players, not a sole controller, and the business is diversified across aerospace, vehicle, and eMobility. Supply response score 7: ramping switchgear and transformer capacity requires 2-5 years due to grain-oriented electrical steel shortages, skilled labor, and certification/testing cycles, but it is not geologically constrained like mining.

name: GE Vernova
constraint_controlled: Dominant manufacturing capacity for heavy-duty gas turbines and high-voltage grid equipment (transformers, switchgear) with multi-year backlogs.
physics_thesis: GE Vernova manufactures the gas turbines, HVDC equipment, and grid hardware that AI data centers and utilities physically require to add generation and transmission capacity. Gas turbine slots are sold out through ~2028, and global capacity to build large-frame turbines is concentrated among only three OEMs (GEV, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi). They also service ~55% of the world's nuclear fleet, giving optionality on nuclear revival.
key_metrics: Gas turbine backlog (GW and $); Power segment book-to-bill; Electrification segment orders growth
reasoning: Ownership score 7 because GEV physically manufactures (not just designs) scarce capital equipment with only 2 real global competitors and multi-year replication time, but it sells equipment rather than operating the power assets itself, and Wind/diversified segments dilute the pure-play exposure. Supply response 8 because adding new heavy gas turbine manufacturing capacity (large castings, specialty alloys, skilled labor) takes 5-10 years even with capital — the bottleneck is real and slow to relieve.

name: Quanta Services
constraint_controlled: Quanta controls the largest skilled linemen workforce and specialized equipment fleet for building electric transmission and distribution infrastructure in North America.
physics_thesis: AI data centers require massive grid buildout, and the binding constraint is not capital but skilled labor — linemen take years to train and unions gate supply. Quanta operates (not just sells) the largest such workforce, executing transmission projects utilities cannot self-perform. As grid capex surges, Quanta's labor pool is a genuine physical bottleneck, though it is a service provider rather than an owner of irreplaceable hard assets.
key_metrics: Electric infrastructure backlog ($B); lineman headcount and apprenticeship pipeline; book-to-bill ratio
reasoning: Ownership score of 6: Quanta directly operates the scarce asset (skilled labor + specialized fleet) rather than just selling equipment, but it does not own irreplaceable physical infrastructure like mines or generation, and competitors (MasTec, MYR Group) exist. Supply response of 8: training journeyman linemen takes 4-7 years, union apprenticeships gate throughput, and this cannot be accelerated meaningfully with capital alone.

name: Hubbell
constraint_controlled: Manufacturing capacity for utility-grade transmission and distribution components (arresters, insulators, connectors, switches, smart meters) feeding constrained grid buildout.
physics_thesis: Hubbell sells critical T&D components into the grid bottleneck that AI data centers face, benefiting from utility capex cycles and transformer/grid equipment shortages. However, Hubbell does not OWN the grid or generation — it is an equipment vendor with real competitors (Eaton, ABB, Siemens, nVent), so it captures the theme indirectly rather than controlling a scarce physical asset.
key_metrics: Utility Solutions segment organic growth; T&D equipment backlog and lead times; utility capex spending YoY
reasoning: Ownership score of 5 reflects that Hubbell is an equipment vendor selling INTO the grid bottleneck rather than owning the physical infrastructure, with multiple credible competitors. Supply response of 6 reflects 2-5 year lead times to expand specialty grid equipment manufacturing (tooling, skilled labor, grain-oriented steel, copper) — real but not insurmountable bottlenecks.

name: Vertiv Holdings
constraint_controlled: Vertiv is the dominant OEM for liquid cooling and integrated power management systems required by high-density AI GPU clusters that physically cannot be air-cooled.
physics_thesis: Blackwell-class and beyond GPUs dissipate heat densities that exceed air-cooling physics, forcing a hard transition to direct-liquid and immersion cooling. Vertiv has the deepest installed base, reference designs co-developed with NVIDIA, and the manufacturing scale for CDUs, rear-door heat exchangers, busbars, and switchgear — components every hyperscaler needs simultaneously. While competitors (Schneider, nVent, Munters) exist, Vertiv's integrated power+thermal stack and lead times give it pricing power as data center thermal load is a non-negotiable physical constraint.
key_metrics: Liquid cooling backlog and book-to-bill; AI-related orders growth YoY; gross margin expansion on thermal segment
reasoning: Ownership score of 9 reflects that Vertiv is explicitly cited as the dominant liquid-cooling supplier in the rubric — it manufactures the irreplaceable thermal infrastructure, though 2-3 credible competitors prevent a perfect 10. Supply response of 6 because while Vertiv itself can scale factories in 2-3 years, qualifying new entrants into hyperscaler reference designs, scaling specialized CDU/manifold manufacturing, and copper/compressor supply chains make rapid substitution difficult.

name: Modine Manufacturing
constraint_controlled: Modine manufactures and operates production capacity for data center cooling systems (CDUs, chillers, air handlers) including the Airedale brand, a key supplier for AI/HPC thermal management.
physics_thesis: AI GPU clusters generate heat densities that mandate purpose-built cooling, and Modine's Airedale division supplies precision air handlers and liquid cooling distribution units directly into hyperscaler builds. While not the dominant liquid-cooling OEM (Vertiv holds that crown), Modine has a fast-growing data center segment with real manufacturing footprint and customer lock-in. The bottleneck is genuine but Modine is one of several credible suppliers, not a sole-source.
key_metrics: Data center segment revenue growth; Airedale order backlog; hyperscaler customer concentration
reasoning: Modine directly manufactures cooling equipment that AI data centers physically require, justifying a 6 — they own the production capacity but face real competition from Vertiv, Trane, Schneider, and Stulz. Supply response is 1-2 years since cooling equipment can be scaled with new factory lines and is not geologically constrained, though specialized liquid-cooling capacity has bottlenecks pushing it toward the 5 band.

name: Cameco
constraint_controlled: Cameco owns and operates Tier-1 uranium mines (Cigar Lake, McArthur River) with the highest-grade uranium reserves in the Western world, plus conversion capacity and a Westinghouse stake.
physics_thesis: AI's power demand is reviving nuclear globally, but uranium mines take 10-20 years to permit and develop, and the West has structurally underinvested for a decade. Cameco controls irreplaceable high-grade Canadian reserves and is one of only a handful of Western producers — there is no substitute material and no fast supply response. Westinghouse adds reactor OEM exposure, doubling the lock on the nuclear value chain.
key_metrics: Uranium spot/term price ($/lb U3O8); Cigar Lake & McArthur production volumes; long-term utility contract book
reasoning: Direct physical ownership of geologically scarce, high-grade uranium reserves with no substitute earns a 10 on ownership — this is the canonical example in the rubric. Supply response is also a 10 because new uranium mines require 10-20 years for exploration, permitting, and development regardless of capital, and the fuel cycle (conversion, enrichment) adds further bottlenecks.

name: Oklo Inc.
constraint_controlled: Oklo is developing Aurora SMR fission powerhouses (15-75MW) but has not yet built or operated any commercial reactor.
physics_thesis: Oklo targets a genuine bottleneck — behind-the-meter nuclear power for AI data centers — and has a notable customer pipeline plus DOE site approval at Idaho National Laboratory. However, it currently OWNS no operating physical asset; its first reactor is not expected online until 2027-2028, and NRC licensing remains incomplete after a prior denial. The thesis is real but speculative: it's a design/developer stage company, not yet a power asset owner.
key_metrics: NRC combined license application status; MW under signed customer agreements; first Aurora commissioning date
reasoning: Ownership score of 5 reflects that Oklo does not yet operate any physical power asset — it is a pre-revenue reactor developer, closer to a designer than an asset owner, despite the strong nuclear thesis. Supply response score of 9 reflects that fission plants, even SMRs, take 5-10+ years to license, fuel (HALEU constrained), and build, and cannot be accelerated meaningfully with capital alone.

name: Freeport-McMoRan
constraint_controlled: Owns and operates some of the world's largest copper mines including Grasberg (Indonesia), Morenci (Arizona), and Cerro Verde (Peru) with decades of proven reserves.
physics_thesis: AI data centers require massive copper for power transmission, transformers, busbars, and wiring — a single GW-scale data center consumes thousands of tons of copper. New copper mines take 10-20 years from discovery to production due to permitting, geology, and capital intensity, and global ore grades are declining. Freeport is the largest publicly-traded pure-play copper producer with irreplaceable in-ground reserves.
key_metrics: Copper production volume (lbs/yr); realized copper price ($/lb); Grasberg underground ramp-up progress
reasoning: Ownership scores 9 because FCX directly operates tier-1 copper assets that cannot be replicated — Grasberg alone is one of the largest copper-gold deposits ever found. Supply response scores 10 because copper mines are the canonical 10-20 year asset; even with unlimited capital, permitting, water rights, and ore body development cannot be compressed.

name: Southern Copper
constraint_controlled: Owns and operates some of the world's largest copper reserves and producing mines in Peru and Mexico, including Toquepala, Cuajone, and Buenavista.
physics_thesis: AI data centers require massive amounts of copper for power transmission, transformers, busbars, and wiring — roughly 50,000+ tons per GW of data center capacity. Southern Copper holds the largest copper reserves of any publicly traded miner, with multi-decade mine lives in tier-1 jurisdictions. New copper mines take 10-20 years to permit and develop, making existing producing assets irreplaceable as AI-driven demand collides with grid electrification.
key_metrics: Copper production volume (Mlb/yr); realized copper price ($/lb); reserve life and grade at Toquepala/Cuajone/Buenavista
reasoning: SCCO directly owns and operates physically scarce, geologically irreplaceable copper deposits — pure physical control of the bottleneck, not equipment or services. Copper supply cannot respond to price signals on AI timescales: permitting, construction, and ramp routinely exceed a decade (e.g., Tia Maria stalled 15+ years), warranting a 10 on supply response. Ownership at 9 rather than 10 because Freeport, BHP, and Codelco are meaningful peers, though SCCO has the largest reserves.

name: Nvidia Corporation
constraint_controlled: NVIDIA controls GPU architecture IP and CUDA software ecosystem, but does not own any fabrication, power, or physical infrastructure.
physics_thesis: NVIDIA is the demand-creator at the top of the AI bottleneck chain, not a controller of physical bottlenecks below it. It is fabless — TSMC manufactures the chips, SK Hynix supplies HBM, and hyperscalers provide power and cooling. Its moat is architectural and software-based (CUDA), not a physically scarce asset that fits the physics arbitrage thesis.
key_metrics: Data center revenue growth; CUDA developer ecosystem size; HBM/CoWoS allocation from TSMC
reasoning: Ownership score of 4 reflects that NVIDIA is fabless and owns no physical bottleneck infrastructure — its scarcity is IP/software, not physics. Supply response of 6 reflects that competitors (AMD, custom ASICs from hyperscalers) need 2-5 years to meaningfully challenge CUDA and the architectural lead, but this is a software/design moat, not a geological or grid-based one.
